title: Town Baby Name Chart
story: Every January, a town newsletter prints the most popular baby names from last year. The registry sends one list with a lowercase name for every baby born, like ["mia", "leo", "mia", "ava"].
The chart shows the top k names, most popular first, with ties listed alphabetically.
task: Write topNames(names, k). Return the k most frequent names, ordered by how many times they appear (highest first). Names with the same count go in alphabetical order.
Each name appears in the result at most once. k is never more than the number of different names.
constraints: Names use only lowercase letters a to z, 1 to 15 letters long.

examples.explanation: mia appears 3 times, leo 2, ava and zoe once each. The top 2 are mia, then leo.
noah, eli and ivy all appear twice, so they tie and are listed alphabetically: eli, ivy, noah. Listing them in the order they first appear (noah, eli, ivy) would be wrong.

hints: Before ranking, what do you need to know about each name, and how do you get it in one pass?
Count each name in a hash map. Now pick the best k distinct names. What does "better" mean when two counts are equal?

One comparison rule: A ranks above B if A has a higher count, or the same count and comes first alphabetically. Sorting every distinct name by it works. Can you avoid sorting names that will never make the chart?

Keep a heap of at most k names with the weakest on top (lowest count; for equal counts, the alphabetically later name). Push each distinct name and pop when the heap passes k. At the end, pop everything (weakest first) and reverse.
bruteForce: Count each distinct name by rescanning the whole list, then sort. That is O(n · m) for n babies and m distinct names, up to 400 million steps for 20,000 all-different names.

A hash map fixes the counting. Sorting all m names by (count, then name) is then O(m log m), fine here. A heap of size k cuts it to O(m log k), which helps when there are many distinct names and the chart is short.

js: * @param {string[]} names  one name per baby, lowercase
* @return {string[]} top k names, most frequent first, ties alphabetical
py: def top_names(names: list[str], k: int) -> list[str]:

tests.note: tie of ones: alphabetical, not first-seen order
k equals the number of distinct names
one name is a prefix of another: shorter comes first alphabetically
tie below the leader decides the last place

js: // weaker(a, b): a ranks below b on the chart
const heap = []; // weakest kept name on top
if (l < heap.length && weaker(heap[l], heap[m])) m = l;
if (r < heap.length && weaker(heap[r], heap[m])) m = r;
if (heap.length > k) pop(); // drop the weakest
py: # Rank key: higher count first, then alphabetical.
# nsmallest keeps a heap of size k internally: O(m log k).
return heapq.nsmallest(k, count, key=lambda n: (-count[n], n))
walkthrough: Count with a hash map, then rank with one rule, "higher count wins; on a tie, the alphabetically earlier name wins", keeping only the best k without sorting everyone.
Trace the second example with k = 3. Counts: noah 2, eli 2, ivy 2, amir 1. The heap keeps the weakest name on top.
• Push eli. Same count, but noah is later alphabetically, so noah is weaker and stays on top.
• Push ivy. noah is still the weakest. Size 3.
• Push amir (count 1). Size 4, so pop the weakest: amir, the only name with count 1.
• Pop everything: noah, ivy, eli (weakest first). Reverse: ["eli", "ivy", "noah"].

The tie rule flips inside the heap: to keep the best names you evict the worst, and among equal counts that is the alphabetically later one. Getting that backwards is the usual bug. Python's heapq.nsmallest with key (-count, name) runs the same size-k heap for you.
solution.timeWhy: Counting is one pass over n names; each of the m distinct names costs O(log k) in the heap.
solution.spaceWhy: The count map holds every distinct name; the heap holds k.
solution.takeaway: For "top k by some score", count with a hash map, then keep a heap of size k ordered by the full ranking rule, tie-break included, with the weakest kept item on top.
